558.name: An overview of art
558.description: In this unit pupils enhance their critical thinking exploring art from various perspectives. They discuss what defines art, study galleries and museums and art's connection to the curriculum. They consider drawing and how emotions are expressed using this medium.
558.why: This unit is useful for pupils as they transition to secondary school, where they will encounter more complex and diverse ideas. By exploring what defines art and examining its role across various contexts, pupils develop critical thinking and analytical skills. This unit encourages them to question and appreciate art's multifaceted nature, preparing them for more advanced art studies. Addressing common challenges like drawing confidence helps build resilience and fosters a growth mindset in their artistic journey.
prior: Pupils know about significant art movements and their historical context
Pupils know a variety of mark making techniques
Pupils know how to use line and tone

559.name: An overview of craft
559.description: This unit explores the world of craft, learning practices and significance, and engaging in handmaking their own projects. Pupils will use specialist materials and tools, research notable craftspeople, and enhance their practical skills and appreciation for craftsmanship.
559.why: This unit introduces pupils to the rich tradition and contemporary practice of craft, broadening their understanding of art beyond conventional fine arts. It builds on their existing skills and encourages hands-on creativity, critical for their development as versatile artists. Understanding craft's role and techniques fosters respect for different art forms and cultivates a comprehensive skill set, preparing pupils for diverse artistic pursuits in secondary school and beyond.
prior: Pupils know how to make objects using a variety of materials and processes
Pupils know the material properties of clay
Pupils know the material properties of a variety of textiles
Pupils know the material properties of paper and card
Pupils have experience of printing techniques

560.name: An overview of design
560.description: This unit helps pupils to define design and understand the roles of designers and architects. They will study traditional and contemporary practices and research influential designers. Lessons will enhance understanding, foster creativity, and develop research and critical thinking skills.
560.why: This unit expands pupils' awareness of real-life creative industries as it introduces them to the vast field of design, which hones the applied aspect of their artistic development. It builds on their existing knowledge and encourages them to think creatively about how design impacts the world around them. Understanding the principles and history of design prepares pupils for more advanced art and design studies, fostering a deep appreciation for the role of design in everyday life.
prior: Pupils know how artists and designers record their environment
Pupils know how artists and designers find inspiration
Pupils know some of the major art and design movements
Pupils know and understand work in three dimensions

564.name: The elements of art
564.description: Pupils will develop an understanding of the basic elements of art and learn how artists use these elements in different ways in their work. In the unit, pupils will answer questions as they look at the elements through a variety of processes to identify how they are used in different art forms.
564.why: In previous units pupils have been introduced to the introductions of Art, Craft and Design. This unit moves into the technical, through the elements of art which form the building blocks of the subject. Looking at each of the elements in turn and how different artforms and artists have interpretted them in their work.
prior: The variety of tools and equipment for making art
Expressive mark making
Basic colour theory
Positive and negative space
Arranging elements of art

561.name: Art movements
561.description: Pupils will analyse and critique a selection of western art movements and understand their wider historical relevance. Pupils will engage with practical tasks to gain an understanding of the defining techniques and materials used as well as writing a manifesto.
561.why: This unit broadens pupils understanding of how the movements connect with a wider historical context. The unit looks at key western art movements in more depth and with chronological awareness. It sets a backdrop for engaging with artworks and artists with more depth of understanding and taking part in analysis and discussions.
prior: Understanding of the broader context and purpose of art and the art world
Familiarity with a sense of chronology and how to order events in chronological order
Experience in engaging with and discussing artworks
Understanding of basic techniques and processes in art

563.name: The importance of nature in art
563.description: In this unit, pupils will explore art, artefacts, and architecture from around the world. Through hands-on activities, they will experiment with different techniques and materials to create artworks. Pupils will gain a wider context of how art shapes and reflects our global history overtime.
563.why: This unit broadens pupils understanding of the relationship between artists in the west and globally. At this stage, students are developing critical thinking and creative skills, making it an ideal time to continue their exploration of a shared language developed between artists from different global perspectives This unit encourages pupils to appreciate different perspectives, fostering a broader worldview and inspiring their own artistic techniques.
prior: Understanding of basic art techniques and materials
Familiarity with global artists and their works
Basic knowledge of global historical periods in art
Awareness of different artistic styles
Ability to describe and analyse artworks

565.name: Textiles and the creative industries
565.description: This unit starts by offering pupils insights into diverse career opportunities within the creative industries, looking at Fashion in more detail. It leads into a textiles unit exploring different elements of textiles and fabric manipulation
565.why: This unit builds on pupils' existing skills by enhancing their ability to research, analyse, and understand the creative industries. Learning about the economic impact and roles of creative institutions enhances their awareness of the broader context of their artistic practice. Investigating creative jobs, networks, and funding opportunities builds on their knowledge of career development and professional practice. Exploring career progression fosters their ability to plan and set goals for their future.
prior: The properties of a variety of materials
Hands on making using a variety of materials
Practical skills using a variety of tools

566.name: Being curious about spatial design and architecture
566.description: Pupils will explore architecture and the built environment, learning about form, volume, domestic and public buildings, cultural structures, and materials. Lessons will enhance understanding of architectural principles, appreciation for styles, and skills in perspective drawing and design.
566.why: This unit introduces pupils to the fundamental concepts and principles of architecture. Building on their existing art skills, pupils will learn to appreciate the built environment and understand the role of architecture in shaping our world. This unit promotes critical thinking, creativity, and an appreciation for cultural and historical contexts. It prepares pupils for more advanced art and design studies by encouraging them to explore complex forms and structures through both theoretical and practical approaches.

567.name: Being curious about 3D design
567.description: Pupils will explore sculptural forms, delving into organic and human made forms through 3D art. They will enhance their 3D thinking, source inspiration, and experiment with various materials. Pupils will learn technical techniques, modeling, and construction methods.
567.why: This unit introduces pupils to three-dimensional thinking and sculptural techniques, building on their existing 3D knowledge and skills. Exploring biomorphic and human made forms encourages a deeper connection with the world around us. Learning to model, construct, and display 3D sculptures prepares pupils for more advanced art projects, fostering a comprehensive understanding of form, space, and texture. This unit promotes creativity, technical skill, and innovative thinking, crucial for development as versatile artists.

568.name: Abstract painting: sustainable materials
568.description: Pupils will develop their understanding of abstract painting and make more sophisticated connections. They will build confidence in taking risks with new ideas, look at different tools and techniques, and learn to communicate with symbols and marks.
568.why: This unit encourages pupils to delve into personal expression and self-discovery through art. Building on their existing skills, pupils will learn to articulate their thoughts, emotions, and experiences visually. This unit promotes emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and creativity. It prepares pupils for more advanced art projects by encouraging them to explore and communicate personal narratives and connections through their work.

570.name: Being curious about printing
570.description: Pupils will develop essential print making skills, explore connections between media and materials. They will learn to control various printmaking tools and be aware of the sustainability of their materials. They will recycle tetrapak and card to make their print blocks.
570.why: This unit supports pupils as they integrate the important concept of sustainability into their artistic practice. Building on their existing skills, pupils will learn to create prints that are environmentally conscious and promotes sustainable practices. This unit promotes critical thinking, innovation, and responsibility. It prepares pupils for future art projects by encouraging them to consider the environmental impact of their work and to think creatively about sustainable solutions.

569.name: Collage and Assemblage: sustainable materials
569.description: Pupils will develop their collaging skills and showcase their strengths. They will learn about the different between using the metholody as part of the process or as the technique. They will explore how to place images together and develop compositional skills as well as be playful with ideas.
569.why: This unit supports pupils as they integrate the important concept of sustainability into their artistic practice. Building on their existing skills, pupils will learn to create collages that are environmentally conscious and promotes sustainable practices. This unit promotes critical thinking, innovation, and responsibility. It prepares pupils for future art projects by encouraging them to consider the environmental impact of their work and to think creatively about sustainable solutions.

608.name: The principles of art
608.description: This unit expands pupils understanding of the foundations of creative practice, building on knowledge of the elements of art, to now explore more complex principles. This will deepen understanding of how artists use these principles to question the world around them and communicate their ideas.
608.why: In previous units pupils have been introduced to the elements of art which form the building blocks of the subject. This unit builds on the elements with the principles of art, in which pupils understand how to critique work using the fundamental concepts. The pupils are able to articulate their thoughts and opinions about artwork using more complex subject specific vocabulary.
prior: Understanding of the elements of art.
Experience of reflection and evaluation.

609.name: Identity: exploring portraiture
609.description: This unit explores portraiture’s power in expressing identity, culture, and belief. Pupils will study artists who challenge stereotypes and explore power, representation, and concealment. They will develop critical thinking while reinforcing respect, tolerance, and self-expression.
609.why: This unit builds on prior learning about identity and draws inspiration from the Equality Act 2010 and protected characteristics. Centered on British values, it fosters pupils’ understanding of their own identity and their right to self-identify, promoting tolerance and respect for diversity. The unit also enhances their art skills and critical thinking while introducing how artists explore identity and challenge stereotypes. It lays the groundwork for future discussions on identity, essential for their progression into GCSE, by scaffolding creative conversations around identity and diversity.
prior: An understanding of concepts related to personal and social identity, including the significance of diversity in society

Ability to contribute to discussions

611.name: Personal identity
611.description: This unit explores personal identity in art through self-expression, mapping, storytelling, and the interplay between personal and universal themes. Pupils will engage with a variety of art forms while considering how identity is shaped and communicated.
611.why: In this final unit before GCSEs it is vital that pupils begin to explore their own sense of self and their own creative desires through various provcations. This unit is situated here to begin to support more independent choice making, allowing for pupils to have more ownership over their learning and creative practice, which is needed at the next level.
prior: How artists seek and find inspiration
How to record thoughts and feelings that can be translated into a visual response
Ability to form and articulate personal opinions appropriately
Ability to access, filter and identify appropriate research information and self reflection

610.name: Social action
610.description: Pupils will explore social action in a variety of forms, from collaborative practice to inndividual action and how art works can challenge ideas and influenece decisions. These lessons encourage critical thinking and self-expression, fostering creativity, empathy, and social awareness.
610.why: This unit deepens pupils understanding of socially engaged art and how creative practitioners tackle important societal issues. Building on their existing skills, pupils will learn to create meaningful and thought-provoking artworks that reflect contemporary concerns. This unit promotes critical thinking, emotional awareness, and an understanding of the role of art in society. It prepares pupils for more advanced art projects by encouraging them to explore complex themes and develop a personal artistic voice.
prior: Knowledge of contemporary art movements and how artists use their work to reflect societal issues.
Basic awareness of current societal concerns such as equality, climate change, or justice, to critically engage with themes explored in socially engaged art.

1588.name: Connections: home, space and family
1588.description: Pupils will explore the theme of family in art and how ideals of what a family is has changed over time. The unit builds on both the history of familial connections in art, as well as exploring contemporary forms of family. Pupils will explore the theme of family through 3d forms.
1588.why: This unit encourages pupils to consider the notion of the family in all of its diversity. This will encourage a deeper reflection and analysis of the various nuances within this theme, at a time when pupils increasingly seek to articulate diverse experiences. This complexity of thought will be needed as they move into their exam years and will be supported creatively through more symbolic forms of communication, as well as being inspired by more sculptural forms of practice.

1589.name: Art for life: expression and belonging
1589.description: Pupils will explore how creative making can support health and wellbeing through personal expression and use art for self-discovery. Inspired by artistic practice they will investigate art as a tool for transformation and connection, using memories and reflections to support a sense of belonging.
1589.why: This unit encourages pupils to delve into personal expression and self-discovery through art. Building on their existing skills, pupils will learn to articulate their thoughts, emotions, and experiences visually. This unit promotes expression, critical thinking, and creativity. It prepares pupils for more advanced art projects by encouraging them to explore and communicate personal narratives and connections through their work.

612.name: Foundation workshops: selecting primary sources and recording observations
612.description: This teacher-led unit introduces key principles and four assessment objectives through various drawing activities in the studio and on-site. Pupils will explore diverse sources, inspired by themes from a museum or site visit.
612.why: This unit is useful for pupils as they move into GCSE or alternative courses, where they will encounter more complex and diverse ideas. Pupils will become more independent in their practice, chosing themes and processes inspired by their own interests and strengths. This unit encourages students to make their own creative decisions, find and create their resources. This empowers the students to judge critically both the quality and relevence of their chosen materials.

1653.name: Foundation workshops: revisiting elements of art and principles of art
1653.description: This unit revisits and reframes the key principles and elements of art. Pupils will study how artists use these elements with greater sophistication. They will carefully examine and analyse the elements and principles, applying them to their chosen art forms and endorsements.
1653.why: This unit is important for pupils at the beginning of the GCSE course to build on their understanding of the building blocks for making art. They will have explored what defines art and examined its role across various contexts, pupils have developed critical thinking and analytical skills. This unit encourages students to make the necessary links between the underyling elements and principles and the work that they, and other artists are making.
prior: Working knowledge of the artistic elements including colour, line, pattern, 2D, 3D and virtual.

1564.name: Fine Art
1564.description: This is a teacher led unit which introduces to pupils to the skills within their endorsements. Through a series of workshop activities, students experiment with a range of materials and techniques. They develop a range of studies exploring mark making media, print and mixed media.
1564.why: This unit builds on pupils' foundational knowledge and skills from previous years, introducing more advanced techniques and processes. By exploring different media, materials, and methods, pupils gain versatility and confidence in their creative abilities. This unit prepares pupils for the diverse challenges of higher-level art projects and encourages them to experiment and innovate. It also emphasises the importance of refining and controlling artistic processes, essential for producing high-quality work.

1785.description: This unit introduces pupils to developing their own voice. They will learn about key components in shaping their artistic voice, including research, reflection and refining ideas. The unit takes them on a journey of discovery leading to planning a final piece.

980.name: First sustained project: working from a theme
980.description: This is an independent, pupil-led unit where pupils develop their own creative process. Having learned the key components of shaping an artistic voice, they will now make choices about themes, techniques, and processes, articulating and evaluating their artistic journey.
980.why: This teacher led unit builds on the previous learning in the curriculum in which pupils have widened their understanding of art, craft and design. They have developed an appreciation of its cultural and historical contexts and have developed their critical thinking, innovation, and taken responsibility for their creative decisions. This is the right point for students to become more independent and make connections with their process and the world around them.

1161.name: Second sustained project: working from a theme changing perspectives
1161.description: This unit introduces collaborative working methods, even when assessed individually. Pupils will work together to respond to a theme, creating first-hand sources, then respond individually. They’ll learn to contribute to larger projects while maintaining their own identity.
1161.why: At this stage, pupils have an increasing awareness of their own developing practice and creative intentions. This unit provides the opportunity for pupils to engage in targeted, intensive practice and experimentation with materials, techniques, and processes. They are beginning to identify key areas for development, focusing on improving technical skills to better realise their intentions. The unit encourages refinement of their ideas and practice, allowing them to explore more advanced approaches to their work while developing greater control over their chosen media and processes.

Casting enables the creation of multiple copies or editions of a sculpture, making art more accessible and versatile.
keywords: multiple copies of a sculpture from one mould
surface treatment (polish, paint, patina) that changes appearance and durability
hollow form used to shape liquid or pliable casting material

6932.name: Mixed media sculptures: combining diverse materials and techniques
6932.outcome: I can choose and combine materials to make a mixed media sculpture that is expressive, integrated and experimental.
points: The choice of materials becomes part of the message; each one can evoke different emotions, histories, or associations.
Successful mixed media sculpture depends on understanding how to physically and visually integrate different materials.
Mixed media expands creative boundaries, encouraging experimentation, recycled elements, or unconventional techniques.
keywords: trying out different styles, materials and compositions to see what works best
the process of adapting to and becoming part of a new society

6934.name: Advancing modelling: shaping with clay
6934.outcome: I can build, shape and add expressive detail to clay, showing movement and emotion.
points: Modelling is a process, where forms are built up by gradually adding and shaping material like clay, wax, or plaster.
Developing sensitivity to moisture levels, structural support, drying times is essential, especially working with clay.
Expressing movement, emotion and narrative through gesture, posture and detail makes work compelling and communicative.
keywords: a substance added to something else to improve or alter it
a movement that helps express an idea or meaning
how a piece of writing is sequenced

7634.name: Drawing skills: digital drawing
7634.outcome: I can create a digital drawing using layers, pressure sensitivity and tonal variation to produce a refined still-life image.
points: Digital drawing software applications provide different techniques for artists and designers.
Layers can be used to organise, edit and refine sections of a digital artwork.
Brush settings and pressure sensitivity can affect mark-making capabilities.
Artistic principles such as composition and proportion can be applied in a digital medium.
keywords: a separate, transparent sheet within a digital canvas used to organise elements of an artwork
controls how transparent or solid an object appears
how tablet pen pressure affects line thickness or opacity

7635.name: Drawing skills: drawing with light
7635.outcome: I can use long exposure photography to create expressive light drawings that demonstrate control of composition and light.
points: Light can be used as a drawing tool in photography.
Long exposure allows movement of light to be captured as lines and shapes.
Composition and planning are key to effective light drawings.
It’s important to consider light sources and plan a light drawing to create an effective image that shows contrast.
keywords: the arrangement of visual elements within an artwork
the difference between elements (like light and dark or rough and smooth) that makes parts of an artwork stand out
the amount of light allowed to hit the light-sensitive surface to create an image
Something that is a light source produces its own light.

7636.name: Drawing skills: drawing with 3D
7636.outcome: I can create a 3D drawing using wire or other materials to represent line, contour and form in space.
points: Drawing can move beyond paper by using materials like wire and string to construct “lines in space”.
3D drawing develops understanding of form, balance and structure.
Materials can be manipulated to suggest contours, proportion and movement.
keywords: a frame or skeleton inside a sculpture that helps it stay up
the act of assembling materials to form a structure or object
the line outlining a shape or form, like an outline
the specific type or category of a poem that determines its structure and style

4763.name: The role and impact of curators
4763.outcome: I can analyse, explain and apply curatorial principles.
points: Curators organise and manage art exhibitions to enhance viewer understanding.
Curators use space and flow to shape how viewers experience art.
Curation involves selecting, arranging, and presenting artworks.
Curators impact how art is perceived and interpreted by the public.
keywords: refers to selecting and organising literature for a specific purpose or audience.
an exhibition is a public show of art, crafts, products, or skills
the way a text is structured

6955.name: Artists as curators
6955.outcome: I can understand that artists can take on the role of curator.
points: Artists may curate exhibitions to maintain control over work and engage audiences in new ways.
Self-curation can challenge traditional power structures in the art world.
In some cases, curation itself becomes part of the artwork.
keywords: what people see, feel, think and do when they visit an exhibition or artwork
an open area where your opponent isn't standing

4762.name: Selecting work and considering the audience
4762.outcome: I can select and present my work so it connects to my theme and engages the audience.
points: Every artwork in an exhibition must reinforce the central theme or concept.
The best selections engage the audience and communicate something meaningful.
A strong exhibition feels unified because each piece complements the others.
keywords: Context concerns the circumstances in which a text was written; context helps us to understand the writer’s intentions further.
in writing, the structure is cohesive if it is clear how the parts fit together. It has a clear introduction, middle and conclusion

6645.name: Presentation of work
6645.outcome: I can present my artwork so it is clear, purposeful, and communicates effectively to audiences.
points: Presentation is part of GCSE assessment and helps examiners see the journey of ideas.
Layout and organisation should guide the viewer through work in a logical sequence.
Annotations should explain why you made artistic decisions, linking them to the theme or concept.
Labels give basic, factual information to the audience.
keywords: written notes that explain, justify, or reflect on artistic decisions
a structured delivery of information, ideas or arguments to an audience

4764.name: Reproducing art: postcards, prints and artist editions
4764.outcome: I can experiment with reproducing and curating my own artwork.
points: Artists can reproduce their work through prints, postcards, and limited edition prints.
There are many examples of artist's reproducing their work in different ways and across different times and places.
A curatorial experiment explores not just which artworks are shown, but how they are arranged, displayed, and framed.
Curators and artists might use reproductions to experiment with how art is displayed and experienced
keywords: multiple copies of a sculpture from one mould
a copy of an original artwork that allows more people to see it

6644.name: Writing an artist statement
6644.outcome: I can create an artist statement that communicates my ideas, materials, and intentions.
points: Traditionally, an artist statement is a piece of writing where artists explain their work, methods, and intentions.
Across history and cultures, artists have explained their work in many different ways.
The statement is part of how art is experienced, it helps the audience engage more deeply.
While traditionally written, it can also take other forms.
keywords: a place in which an artist explains their work, ideas, and methods
the creative goal or message you want your work to express

6954.name: Talking about your work
6954.outcome: I can talk confidently about my artwork, explaining my ideas, process, and intention.
points: Talking about artwork helps the artist and the audience understand ideas, process, and intention.
Verbal explanations can occur in informal conversations or formal presentations.
Reflecting on and discussing artwork helps develop critical thinking and clarity of expression.
Linking materials, techniques, and artistic choices to ideas deepens understanding of the work.
keywords: how others interact with or understand your work
the process of advertising and communicating a strategy to attract a larger audience

4765.name: Promotions: how to publicise a show
4765.outcome: I can use posters and other creative methods to promote an art exhibition.
points: There are different ways to promote an art exhibition or show.
Promotional content uses images, words, and designs that catch attention and share key information.
Posters are not the only method to promote an exhibition, but they are one of the most accessible and versatile ways.
keywords: a visual display used to catch attention, share information, and promote an event, artwork, or idea
a public presentation of artwork (such as an exhibition or performance) where artists display their work for an audience to view, experience, and respond to

395.belief: Art can only be made by one artist, working alone.
395.statement: Art can only be made by one artist, working alone.
395.correction: Art can be a collaborative process. When artists collaborate, they work together to communicate common meanings or achieve common goals.

2497.belief: Drawing has to be a replica of what is being looked at.
2497.statement: Drawing has to be a replica of what is being looked at.
2497.correction: Drawing can be detailed and replicate an object, but it can also be many other things. Artists often play with techniques and process to try out different ways of exploring drawing and this can lead to experimental and exciting discoveries.

392.belief: Art must be created with the hands.
392.statement: Art must be created with the hands.
392.correction: Art is for everyone whatever their circumstances and is not always created through using hands. Artists can create art in innovative ways without using hands. Art is a way for all of humanity to express their viewpoints and diverse experiences.

446.belief: All artworks about causes are created to warn audiences.
446.statement: All artworks about causes are created to warn audiences.
446.correction: There are many reasons why artists make artworks about causes including to bring joy, to celebrate and to inspire hope.

401.belief: Art should be something we instantly recognise and physically last a long time.
401.statement: Art should be something we instantly recognise and physically last a long time.
401.correction: Art may not be a recognisable image and may exist only in a specific timeframe.

443.belief: All of the artwork held in public institutions within the United Kingdom originates from there.
443.statement: All of the artwork held in public institutions within the United Kingdom originates from there.
443.correction: Some artwork held in the collections of public institutions in the UK were created by civilisations that were colonised by the British Empire.

2091.belief: Craft is only about making functional objects and is less important than Fine Art.
2091.statement: Craft is only about making functional objects and is less important than Fine Art.
2091.correction: Craft is the creation of objects and artworks requiring both artistry and technical skill. It includes both functional and non-functional items and embraces contributions from all genders and communities.

10965.belief: Weaving is simply a way of creating fabric for clothing and has no connection to colour or culture.
10965.statement: Weaving is simply a way of creating fabric for clothing and has no connection to colour or culture.
10965.correction: Weaving goes beyond just making fabric; it’s a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.

700.belief: Body adornment is only about appearance or fashion trends.
700.statement: Body adornment is only about appearance or fashion trends.
700.correction: Body adornment often holds deep cultural, religious, or personal meaning. It can express identity, heritage, beliefs, or social status, connecting individuals to family traditions or cultural values— beyond just aesthetic appeal.

5744.belief: Pottery is only used for making practical items like bowls and pots, and it doesn’t have any artistic or cultural significance.
5744.statement: Pottery is only used for making practical items like bowls and pots, and it doesn’t have any artistic or cultural significance.
5744.correction: While pottery is often associated with functional items like bowls and vases, it has been used throughout history and in contemporary times as a medium for artistic expression and storytelling.

8724.belief: Quilts are just blankets or decorative items and don’t have any deeper meaning.
8724.statement: Quilts are just blankets or decorative items and don’t have any deeper meaning.
8724.correction: While quilts are often used for warmth or decoration, many artists use quilts to share powerful stories and messages. Quilts can be a way for artists to speak out about important issues and make sure voices are heard.

8673.belief: Puppets are only used for children's entertainment.
8673.statement: Puppets are only used for children's entertainment.
8673.correction: Different cultures use puppets to tell important stories, share cultural traditions, perform rituals, and even address social or political issues. Puppets can express powerful ideas and emotions, not just for fun but also to convey deeper messages.

2285.belief: Design is about making things that have never been made before.
2285.statement: Design is about making things that have never been made before.
2285.correction: Design is about planning and making something. It doesn’t need to be something that has never been done before, it can be to improve an existing object to make it work or look better.

9219.belief: Set designers work only in theatre and film.
9219.statement: Set designers work only in theatre and film.
9219.correction: Set design is used in many different contexts, including theatre, film, fashion, art and music.

4353.belief: The main role of graphic designers is to make work that is pleasing to the viewer’s eye.
4353.statement: The main role of graphic designers is to make work that is pleasing to the viewer’s eye.
4353.correction: Many graphic designers push traditional boundaries and shift the focus from creating purely aesthetically pleasing works to communicating messages about social justice.

2932.belief: Fashion design is solely about trends and superficial appearances.
2932.statement: Fashion design is solely about trends and superficial appearances.
2932.correction: Fashion design is more than trends; it can challenge our understanding of fashion.

363.belief: Architecture is plain and without details.
363.statement: Architecture is plain and without details.
363.correction: Architects use many different patterns in their designs, both literal patterns and patterns through their use of form.

5813.belief: Printed textile is only for mass production.
5813.statement: Printed textile is only for mass production.
5813.correction: Printed textiles can be produced in limited quantities or even one-of-a-kind pieces.

1882.belief: Composition is only used in one way to express realistic images.
1882.statement: Composition is only used in one way to express realistic images.
1882.correction: Composition is used by artists in many ways, and how composition is used can change across cultures.

4204.belief: Line is only used for drawing.
4204.statement: Line is only used for drawing.
4204.correction: Artists create and apply lines in a multitude of ways across different mediums including sculpture and painting, as well as in drawing.

10350.belief: Tone is all about smooth blending.
10350.statement: Tone is all about smooth blending
10350.correction: Tone can be captured in a variety of ways and mediums

1764.belief: Colours carry the same meaning for everybody.
1764.statement: Colours carry the same meaning for everybody.
1764.correction: Colours can carry different meanings, and these can vary across people, places and cultures.

9240.belief: Shape and form are the same thing.
9240.statement: Shape and form are the same thing.
9240.correction: Shape is flat and 2D, like a drawing. Form is 3D and has depth — you can see or feel it from different angles.

10213.belief: Texture is only about how something feels, not how it looks.
10213.statement: Texture is only about how something feels, not how it looks.
10213.correction: Texture can mean how something feels, and we call that physical texture. But artists can also create the illusion of texture in drawings or paintings — that’s called visual texture.

8888.belief: A repeated pattern is just the same shape copied over and over again.
8888.statement: A repeated pattern is just the same shape copied over and over again.
8888.correction: While repeating the same shape is one way to create a pattern, artists and designers use a variety of methods to make repeated patterns more dynamic, engaging and sophisticated.

2119.belief: Critical thinking focuses on judging artworks as 'good' or 'bad'.
2119.statement: Critical thinking focuses on judging artworks as 'good' or 'bad'.
2119.correction: Critical thinking helps artists and audiences to think deeply about art and respect different viewpoints.

400.belief: Art movements came about in isolation from the world around them.
400.statement: Art movements came about in isolation from the world around them.
400.correction: Art movements are often impacted by changes in the world around them.

440.correction: Artists can make art using many different disciplines.

430.belief: When artists respond to events, they always do so to document that point in history.
430.statement: When artists respond to events, they always do so to document that point in history.
430.correction: There are many ways and reasons why artists respond to events. One of these can be to document that point in history but they can also do so to express their opinions, be a powerful voice for marginalised groups and to help fight for justice.

3576.belief: Iconic images come from across all areas of art history.
3576.statement: Iconic images come from across all areas of art history.
3576.correction: Iconic images mainly come from Western art history which can mean that the diversity of our world is often not reflected.

4408.belief: Manifestos are always communicated through text.
4408.statement: Manifestos are always communicated through text.
4408.correction: In art, manifestos don’t need to be written but can be multidisciplinary in their approach.

418.belief: Artists inspired by nature can only look carefully at natural forms and record them.
418.statement: Artists inspired by nature can only look carefully at natural forms and record them.
418.correction: Artists can make art in and with nature as well as recording from nature.

308.belief: Animals are universially known for specific charatristics across all cultures.
308.statement: Animals are universially known for specific charatristics across all cultures.
308.correction: Often how animals are linked to charateristics in the West is very different that other cultures across the world.

1868.belief: Only complex images or shapes can create associations.
1868.statement: Only complex images or shapes can create associations.
1868.correction: Simple images or shapes can create associations to themes or ideas.

4940.belief: There are no new ways to be inspired by nature.
4940.statement: There are no new ways to be inspired by nature.
4940.correction: We can all find new things that inspire us in the world around us.

426.belief: Artists only make work that looks good and is uplifting.
426.statement: Artists only make work that looks good and is uplifting.
426.correction: Artists use the power of imagery to communicate difficult realities about the planet.

4482.belief: The material of an artwork cannot communicate meaning.
4482.statement: The material of an artwork cannot communicate meaning.
4482.correction: Many artists carefully select materials to deepen the meaning of their work. The materials chosen for an artwork can often communicate meaning through common associations or contextual connections.

2934.correction: Fashion illustrators draw designs and ideas. They help fashion designers show what clothes will look like before they are made.

10322.belief: Tie-dye is a modern European technique.
10322.statement: Tie-dye is a modern European technique
10322.correction: Tie-dye or similar forms, such as Bandhani from India, originates from many different regions around the world and exists in multiple forms and styles. Tie-dye is a global textile technique that has existed for thousands of years.

10151.belief: In Tataki-zome, you should hammer the leaves and flowers as hard as possible to get the best results.
10151.statement: In Tataki-zome, you should hammer the leaves and flowers as hard as possible to get the best results.
10151.correction: Hammering too hard can damage the fabric or crush the plant too much, causing it to bleed or smudge. In Tataki-zome, it’s important to tap gently and evenly so the natural colours and delicate shapes of the plants transfer clearly and beautifully.

2634.belief: Embroidery is a simple way of decorating cloth and has no cultural context.
2634.statement: Embroidery is a simple way of decorating cloth and has no cultural context.
2634.correction: Embroidery goes beyond just being a decorative process, it is a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.

343.belief: Appliqué is just a form of decorating fabric and has no connection to colour or culture.
343.statement: Appliqué is just a form of decorating fabric and has no connection to colour or culture.
343.correction: Appliqué goes beyond just decorating fabric, it's a powerful form of art that can reflect cultural heritage.

775.belief: Buildings are all rectangular in shape with pitched roofs and walls the same colour.
775.statement: Buildings are all rectangular in shape with pitched roofs and walls the same colour.
775.correction: Buildings are made in lots of different shapes and sizes, and are often decorated in ways that are personal to their communities.

774.belief: Buildings are all made from solid materials, brick, stone or concrete.
774.statement: Buildings are all made from solid materials, brick, stone or concrete.
774.correction: Buildings can be constructed from different materials. These may include traditional stone and brick or modern sustainable materials.

776.belief: All buildings have straight lines and are built out of box like shapes.
776.statement: All buildings have straight lines and are built out of box like shapes.
776.correction: Buildings can come in many different forms, with influences coming from a range of different sources.

1762.belief: Colour is just used to make a space look good.
1762.statement: Colour is just used to make a space look good.
1762.correction: Colour in a room can have a big impact on the way a space feels and how we feel in that space.

9782.statement: Students often place the vanishing point too low or high, or forget to use it consistently, which causes the drawing to look distorted or unrealistic.
9782.correction: Remember: the vanishing point sits on the horizon line, which is your eye level. All diagonal lines must meet at the vanishing point—even if it’s off the paper!

9916.belief: Pitching means just reading out facts about the design.
9916.statement: Some students think pitching means just reading out facts about the design.
9916.correction: A strong pitch is more than just facts. It’s a story with a clear beginning, middle and end that shows your idea solves a problem and stands out from the rest.

9142.belief: Sculptures have to be heavy, strong objects which are fully free standing.
9142.statement: Sculptures have to be heavy, strong objects which are fully free standing.
9142.correction: Some sculptures are delicate and light. Sculptural works can be presented in a range of ways including hung, free standing, stacked or in relief.

380.belief: Aritsts can only take direct inspiration from nature, copying it exactly.
380.statement: Aritsts can only take direct inspiration from nature, copying it exactly.
380.correction: Artists have always taken inspiration from nature and can use this as a starting point to develop into complex works.

10063.belief: If the surface is carved too deeply, layers can be glued back on later.
10063.statement: If the surface is carved too deeply, layers can be glued back on later.
10063.correction: Soap is a soft material, and carving too deeply can cause unintended breakage. It’s important to carve in gradual layers, starting with rough shaping before adding finer details.

5567.belief: Plaster and paper will behave the same way in a mould.
5567.statement: Plaster and paper will behave the same way in a mould.
5567.correction: Plaster and paper have very different properties. Plaster sets quickly and picks up fine details. Paper air dries more slowly and shrinks more as it dries. It might not show fine texture as clearly.

1699.belief: Clay work is only about making a vessel which is perfectly symmetrical and with a uniform form.
1699.statement: Clay work is only about making a vessel which is perfectly symmetrical and with a uniform form.
1699.correction: Clay is expressive! It doesn't have to be perfectly symmetrical or realistic. Many artists use bold designs, patterns, and personal storytelling in their work, imperfections add character and meaning.

9144.belief: Sculptures must take a long time to create.
9144.statement: Sculptures must take a long time to create.
9144.correction: Some sculptural works can be quick responsive works.

56.belief: Abstract art is easy to create.
56.statement: Abstract art is easy to create.
56.correction: Abstract art does not try to show things as they look in real life. Instead, it focuses on expressing emotions, ideas, or movement which is not an easy task.

5302.belief: All paintings are made with paint brushes.
5302.statement: All paintings are made with paint brushes.
5302.correction: Using different types of tools helps abstract artists create lots of different types of expressive marks and textures in their work.

5058.belief: When observing a stimulus, it is best to respond using pencil.
5058.statement: When observing a stimulus, it is best to respond using pencil.
5058.correction: Different stimuli, call for different methods like, loose washes, impasto, detailed line work, collage, etc. Matching technique to stimuli ensures the artwork communicates its idea effectively.

431.belief: Artists start a painting or drawing on a plain piece of paper.
431.statement: Artists start a painting or drawing on a plain piece of paper
431.correction: Often artists create surfaces and backgrounds to work on, it makes the piece have less gaps and is interesting to work over.

4466.belief: Mark-making is only needed in abstract work.
4466.statement: Mark-making is only needed in abstract work.
4466.correction: Artists use different marks to express emotions, create mood, and bring their artwork to life.

94.belief: You should only add layers to a painting with paint.
94.statement: You should only add layers to a painting with paint.
94.correction: Dry materials can be used in a variety of ways to add detail and shading to an art work. Dry materials can be layered over the top of wet materials once dried. Examples include pastel over watercolour or pen over dried ink washes.

5816.belief: Printmaking is only about making copies, not about creativity.
5816.statement: Printmaking is only about making copies, not about creativity.
5816.correction: Printmaking is a form of artistic expression, artists can use printmaking to create unique, creative works where textures, colours, and styles can vary greatly.

10500.belief: All types of monoprinting follow the exact same process.
10500.statement: All types of monoprinting follow the exact same process.
10500.correction: There are a number of methods for monoprinting that have different steps and outcomes.

5817.belief: Printmaking requires the use of specialist equipment to be successful.
5817.statement: Printmaking requires the use of specialist equipment to be successful.
5817.correction: High quality printing making can be achieved using a range of domestic materials and equipment.

5086.belief: Once ink is applied to the plate, the design is fixed and cannot be changed.
5086.statement: Once ink is applied to the plate, the design is fixed and cannot be changed.
5086.correction: The printing process is about trying and adjusting. Artists can refine their design through trial and error, removing layers of ink or adding new ones to adjust their composition. It’s important to approach the process with flexibility and patience.

5818.belief: Prints look exactly the same each time you repeat them.
5818.statement: Prints look exactly the same each time you repeat them.
5818.correction: No two prints are exactly alike, even if they come from the same plate or block. Factors like pressure, ink distribution, and the surface it’s printed on can make each print slightly different.

5099.belief: Once a print is made, it’s finished, and no further changes can be made.
5099.statement: Once a print is made, it’s finished, and no further changes can be made.
5099.correction: Prints can be developed further using mixed media and physical alterations like cutting. The process of refining a print is an important step to enhance visual interest and highlight specific areas, creativity doesn't stop after the initial print!

1755.belief: Collage is just about sticking random images together.
1755.statement: Collage is just about sticking random images together.
1755.correction: Collage is about careful selection, layering and composition to create meaning, tell stories, represent identity and explore social themes.

456.belief: Assemblage has to look like a recognisable scene to share meaning with the audience.
456.statement: Assemblage has to look like a recognisable scene to share meaning with the audience.
456.correction: Meaning can be represented through objects, textures, and symbols. The way objects are arranged, and their relationships to each other can all convey emotions, experiences, and personality traits. Assemblage is about meaning, not just likeness.

1753.belief: Collage landscapes should always look realistic.
1753.statement: Collage landscapes should always look realistic.
1753.correction: Collage allows us to create landscapes that don’t have to follow real world rules. Surreal landscapes encourage imagination and creativity beyond what we see in everyday life.

5532.belief: Planning a collage or assemblage takes away creativity.
5532.statement: Planning a collage or assemblage takes away creativity.
5532.correction: Planning provides structure but doesn’t mean the design is fixed. Many artists start with an idea but adapt it through experimentation. A plan helps build confidence, but the best results often come from unexpected discoveries along the way.

1754.belief: Collage is a set process that cannot be modified or refined.
1754.statement: Collage is a set process that cannot be modified or refined.
1754.correction: Collage is a flexible process. Rearranging elements helps refine ideas and create a stronger final piece. Professional artists often make changes mid-process to improve composition and meaning.

57.belief: Abstract collages need to have perfect symmetry or recognisable shapes.
57.statement: Abstract collages need to have perfect symmetry or recognisable shapes.
57.correction: Abstract collages don’t need symmetry or recognisable images. The beauty of abstraction lies in experimenting to create something visually engaging which can express ideas or emotions and finding balance through the arrangement.

9115.correction: Scale is specifically about relative size.

5886.belief: Proportions are set rules and always apply.
5886.statement: Proportions are set rules and always apply
5886.correction: Proportions are relative to the unique form you are observing. They relate to the different sizes of the different parts but may be different for each person, place or object

2102.belief: To create unity, all elements in a piece must look exactly the same or be repeated in a uniform manner.
2102.statement: To create unity, all elements in a piece must look exactly the same or be repeated in a uniform manner.
2102.correction: Variety can still contribute to a cohesive composition, as does repeating elements in a non-uniform way.

442.belief: For artwork to employ variety, it needs to be overwhelming or not unified.
442.statement: For artwork to employ variety, it needs to be overwhelming or not unified.
442.correction: Artwork that employs variety can do so in a unified way to still create work that is cohesive.

8942.belief: Rhythm is just another way of saying pattern.
8942.statement: Rhythm is just another way of saying pattern
8942.correction: Rhythm is a visual beat that utilises pattern and repetition across an artwork to direct your eye across the work.

5044.belief: An object has the same mass whether in real life or in a 2D representation.
5044.statement: An object has the same mass whether in real life or in a 2D representation.
5044.correction: Whilst an object in real life may have a certain physical mass, if it is depicted in an image its visual weight might not represent this physical mass accurately. Especially compared to other items. This is due to the use of visual elements.

482.correction: Asymmetrical designs can use visual weight to create a type of balance even if the work is different on both sides.

4214.belief: Lines create an edge but they don't create volume.
4214.statement: Lines create an edge but they don't create volume.
4214.correction: Contour lines and directional hatching lines can be used to describe the volume of a 3D object in a 2D drawing.

10474.belief: In two point perspective, some lines don't need to recede to the vanishing point.
10474.statement: In two point perspective, some lines don't need to recede to the vanishing point
10474.correction: All lines recede to one of the vanishing points. Otherwise your drawing won't be realistic

2249.belief: Depth can only be created in a realistic scene or in a realistic way.
2249.statement: Depth can only be created in a realistic scene or in a realistic way.
2249.correction: Depth can be entirely imaginary or realistic. Artists can manipulate elements to create the illusion of shapes, colours and lines standing out or recessing in an image.

5714.belief: Portraits must always show the person directly.
5714.statement: Portraits must always show the person directly.
5714.correction: A portrait can also include symbolic representations, like objects that reflect the person’s personality or even something as unique as a sample of their DNA.

5300.belief: The painted portrait only focuses on realism and accuracy in depicting the subject.
5300.statement: The painted portrait only focuses on realism and accuracy in depicting the subject.
5300.correction: While many portraits aim for realism, painting also allows for abstract and emotional interpretations, capturing the subject's personality, mood, and deeper meaning beyond just physical appearance.

4025.belief: Only large, figurative sculptures are considered 3D portraits.
4025.statement: Only large, figurative sculptures are considered 3D portraits.
4025.correction: 3D portraits can be created in various sizes and forms, not just large figurative sculptures. They can include small, detailed works or abstract representations.

4914.belief: Negative space just means there’s nothing there — it’s empty or unfinished.
4914.statement: Negative space just means there’s nothing there — it’s empty or unfinished
4914.correction: Negative space may look ‘empty,’ but artists use it intentionally to draw attention elsewhere — it helps us focus on shape, emotion, or story without showing everything. It’s a powerful choice, not a mistake.

4390.belief: Making a portrait always means painting a face.
4390.statement: Making a portrait always means painting a face.
4390.correction: Artists use paper, cardboard, silhouettes and even walls to create bold, powerful and expressive figures. You do not need to only paint a face to create a portrait.

11091.belief: Words don’t matter that much — it’s the drawing that tells the story.
11091.statement: Words don’t matter that much — it’s the drawing that tells the story.
11091.correction: Words can express things a face alone might not show — like beliefs, experiences, or emotions. The style of the text also adds meaning.

425.belief: When artists make work about identity, they reveal all aspects of themselves.
425.statement: When artists make work about identity, they reveal all aspects of themselves.
425.correction: Artists make selections about what to conceal or reveal in their work.

4454.correction: Artists might use mapping through literal geography, map-like work or more abstract or subjective representations of movement, memory, and relationships.

421.belief: All artists make art with the intention of sharing with an audience.
421.statement: All artists make art with the intention of sharing with an audience.
421.correction: Some art is made as an act of pure self-expression. Even deeply personal works are shaped by history, identity, and society, meaning they can take on wider meanings even if the artist did not intend them to.

390.belief: Art only connects people if everyone understands it the same way.
390.statement: Art only connects people if everyone understands it the same way.
390.correction: Art connects people because it sparks emotions and ideas, even if everyone sees it differently. It’s the shared experience, not exact understanding, that brings people together.

3222.belief: Gender and sexuality are the same thing.
3222.statement: That gender and sexuality are the same thing.
3222.correction: Gender is about your personal identity, how you see yourself, while sexuality is about who you are attracted to.

8866.belief: Religious art only includes paintings or sculptures.
8866.statement: Religious art only includes paintings or sculptures.
8866.correction: Religious art isn’t just paintings or sculptures, it includes architecture, textiles, calligraphy and even temporary creations like Rangoli and sand mandalas, all used to express and connect with the spiritual.

9386.belief: Social action art must always make tangible improvements to an issue.
9386.statement: Social action art must always make tangible improvements to an issue.
9386.correction: Social action art might make tangible improvements to an issue but might focus instead on sparking conversation or raising awareness.

1751.belief: Collaborative art is just a group project with a leader.
1751.statement: Collaborative art is just a group project with a leader.
1751.correction: Collaborative art is a collective process of co-creation where ideas and efforts are deeply intertwined.

402.belief: Art about war mainly glorifies violence or heroism.
402.statement: Art about war mainly glorifies violence or heroism.
402.correction: Much art inspired by war actually critiques violence, depicts the horrors of war, and emphasises the human cost.

445.belief: Artwork is often seen as a passive object that hangs on a wall.
445.statement: Artwork is often seen as a passive object that hangs on a wall.
445.correction: Art can also be used to activate social change and is a process that can helps spark conversation and raise awareness. The act of creating and sharing the work is powerful in itself.

9636.belief: Street art is primarily an illegal activity or act of vandalism.
9636.statement: Street art is primarily an illegal activity or act of vandalism.
9636.correction: Street art is a legitimate and powerful form of artistic expression that addresses important social issues.

360.belief: Architects only consider one building, not the wider area.
360.statement: Architects only consider one building, not the wider area.
360.correction: Architects consider the built environment, the local area's history and needs and think outside the box to create connections between communities in their work.

5487.belief: Pets are not part of a family because they are animals.
5487.statement: Pets are not part of a family because they are animals.
5487.correction: Many people give their pets names, celebrate their birthdays, and care for them every day. Pets can be part of the family.

1795.belief: A common misconception about murals is that they are only decorative.
1795.statement: A common misconception about murals is that they are only decorative.
1795.correction: They often carry powerful social, cultural, or political messages.

8838.belief: Refugees are illegal and take jobs away from others.
8838.statement: Refugees are illegal and take jobs away from others.
8838.correction: Refugees are protected under international law and have the right to seek asylum. While they may need help when they arrive in a new country, many refugees go on to contribute positively to their communities.

11198.belief: Your future identity is completely determined by your family roots.
11198.statement: Your future identity is completely determined by your family roots.
11198.correction: A common misconception is thinking your family roots completely decide who you are, without any chance to grow or change. In truth, your identity is shaped by both your roots and your own experiences.

966.belief: Every child has their own bedroom.
966.statement: Every child has their own bedroom.
966.correction: It’s a common misconception that every child has their own bedroom. In reality, many children share rooms, sleep in a living area or move around different homes.

2111.belief: A crest is for royalty only.
2111.statement: A crest is for royalty only.
2111.correction: Crests are symbols used by families, groups, or communities to represent their identity, values and stories. They are not only for royalty, but for anyone who wants to show their heritage or what they stand for.

10279.belief: Everyone else's emotional state is as it appear to be.
10279.statement: Thinking that everyone else's emotional state is as it appear to be.
10279.correction: People can’t support you if they don’t know you need it. When someone wears an emotional mask, it’s hard to know the real person.

2479.belief: Doodling is not a valid artform.
2479.statement: Doodling is not a valid artform.
2479.correction: Doodling can express emotion, personality and imagination through simple lines and shapes. Many professional artists, illustrators, and designers start their ideas through doodling.

4557.belief: Memories cannot be used to express a person's identity.
4557.statement: Memories cannot be used to express a person's identity
4557.correction: Memories play a key role in shaping who we are as they help us understand our past, influence how we view ourselves and guide how we express our identity over time.

3074.belief: Food is only for eating and cannot be used as an art medium.
3074.statement: Food is only for eating and cannot be used as an art medium.
3074.correction: Food can be used as an art medium because it evokes the senses and carries deep cultural and emotional meanings.

439.belief: Artists always work alone to create their art.
439.statement: Artists always work alone to create their art.
439.correction: Many artists collaborate with others, work in teams, or invite the community to be part of the process.

4556.belief: Memories are always accurate and unchanging.
4556.statement: Memories are always accurate and unchanging.
4556.correction: A common misconception about memories is that they are perfect and unchanging when in reality, memories can be inaccurate, influenced by emotions and change over time.

415.belief: Artists always have a fixed idea before they start their work.
415.statement: Artists always have a fixed idea before they start their work.
415.correction: Many artists gather inspiration as they go. Collecting a wide range of visual sources lets ideas evolve naturally rather than sticking to a single idea.

2864.belief: Exploring different perspectives just means drawing the object from different angles.
2864.statement: Exploring different perspectives just means drawing the object from different angles.
2864.correction: To explore perspectives, you also need to change how you look at the object—by positioning yourself differently, changing your distance, or experimenting with different materials and techniques. It's about seeing the object in new ways.

10704.belief: Using inspiration from artists means copying their work exactly.
10704.statement: Using inspiration from artists means copying their work exactly.
10704.correction: The goal is not to copy an artist's work but to adapt their techniques, mark-making, or approach to develop your own creative style and ideas.

2118.belief: Critical analysis in art is just about writing facts about artists.
2118.statement: Critical analysis in art is just about writing facts about artists.
2118.correction: Critical analysis goes beyond facts; it involves interpreting the artwork, understanding its context, and evaluating its impact and meaning.

10751.belief: Using unconventional materials doesn’t have a deeper purpose in the drawing process.
10751.statement: Using unconventional materials doesn’t have a deeper purpose in the drawing process.
10751.correction: Unconventional materials can lead to unique textures, effects, and creative outcomes, challenging traditional drawing methods.

2495.belief: Drawing always has to be neat, precise, and done with traditional materials like pencil.
2495.statement: Drawing always has to be neat, precise, and done with traditional materials like pencil.
2495.correction: Artists can experiment with non-traditional materials and looser techniques like splashes, drips and sprays to develop freedom and unexpected results.

2424.belief: Distorting a photograph with manipulation techniques only damages it.
2424.statement: Distorting a photograph with manipulation techniques only damages it.
2424.correction: In art, photos are not just static records of the past; they are versatile tools that can be reinterpreted and manipulated to express new ideas and perspectives.

26.belief: 2D drawings cannot be transformed into 3D forms.
26.statement: 2D drawings cannot be transformed into 3D forms.
26.correction: 2D drawings are like a blueprint for 3D forms. By imagining how shapes in a drawing could extend into space, students can add depth, volume, and perspective to give their designs a 3D appearance.

2441.belief: Documenting an artist’s journey is only about completed artworks.
2441.statement: Documenting an artist’s journey is only about completed artworks.
2441.correction: Sketchbooks, notes, and drafts are just as important, showing the development of ideas, experimentation, and problem-solving along the way.

2858.belief: Experiments should include radical or very exaggerated changes.
2858.statement: Experiments should include radical or very exaggerated changes.
2858.correction: You can make very subtle changes and experiements and they can have a big impact on your work - that's the value of experimentation!

11200.belief: Your work needs to be full of obvious pattern for it to feel unified.
11200.statement: Your work needs to be full of obvious pattern for it to feel unified.
11200.correction: Pattern is an important element in art but unity can be felt without artwork looking like a repeat pattern.

36.belief: In 3D or sculptural work, mass is just about how much it weighs and its physical presence.
36.statement: In 3D or sculptural work, mass is just about how much it weighs and its physical presence.
36.correction: Mass can be symbolic due to the materials used. Materials can carry more or less visual weight.

4218.belief: Lines are only useful in drawing and painting.
4218.statement: Lines are only useful in drawing and painting
4218.correction: Lines are vital for all work across every specialism. There are many ways line can impact your work.

3547.belief: Hue and colour mean the same thing.
3547.statement: Hue and colour mean the same thing.
3547.correction: Colour is the overarching name for what we see but it is made up of hues and tones.

9246.belief: Shapes are only found in the positive space made by an actual object.
9246.statement: Shapes are only found in the positive space made by an actual object.
9246.correction: Shapes are inadvertently created all the time in the gaps between objects in your composition. We call this the negative space.

10215.belief: Texture is only a visual quality, it doesn't add meaning to your work.
10215.statement: Texture is only a visual quality, it doesn't add meaning to your work.
10215.correction: Texture is one of the tools artists use as a visual language to communicate.

5374.belief: Patterns need to be regular and ordered.
5374.statement: Patterns need to be regular and ordered.
5374.correction: Pattern can be irregular or regular.

386.belief: The arrangement of the elements has no effect on the overall effectiveness of the composition.
386.statement: The arrangement of the elements has no effect on the overall effectiveness of the composition.
386.correction: A successful composition creates structure and activates the visual language to convey meaning.

956.belief: Charcoal is messy and hard to control, so it's not suitable for detailed or serious artwork.
956.statement: Charcoal is messy and hard to control, so it's not suitable for detailed or serious artwork.
956.correction: While charcoal can be loose and expressive, with practice it can also be controlled for fine detail. Artists often use different types of charcoal (e.g. vine for light sketching, compressed for deep blacks) to achieve a full range of effects.

3017.belief: All fine liners produce the same effect, regardless of nib size.
3017.statement: All fine liners produce the same effect, regardless of nib size.
3017.correction: Nib size changes line weight and impacts detail and clarity; thinner nibs are better for intricate details, thicker nibs for bold outlines.

5085.belief: Once ink is applied it can't be lightened as it is permanent.
5085.statement: Once ink is applied it can't be lightened as it is permanent.
5085.correction: While ink is permanent when dry, it can be diluted with water whilst wet to create lighter values, washes, and gradients.

552.belief: The base layer doesn't matter in painting.
552.statement: The base layer doesn't matter in painting.
552.correction: A strong base layer, or ground, sets tone, mood, and unity. It can shape the whole piece visually and emotionally.

4354.belief: The main subject photo should completely dominate the composition.
4354.statement: The main subject photo should completely dominate the composition.
4354.correction: The photograph should interact with the background, not overpower it. The transparency of acetate or digital opacity allows the viewer to still appreciate the layers beneath. The photograph should complement the painted background, not mask it.

5815.belief: Printmaking has to follow strict rules and can’t be creative or experimental.
5815.statement: Printmaking has to follow strict rules and can’t be creative or experimental.
5815.correction: Artists can experiment with texture, layering, colour and materials; like using different surfaces to print onto or combining different printing methods, to develop unique and expressive outcomes.

4376.belief: You can make multiple identical prints from one monotype plate.
4376.statement: You can make multiple identical prints from one monotype plate.
4376.correction: Monotypes create a single, original image. You can sometimes pull a faint ghost print after the first, but it’s never identical. The unique nature is what makes monotype special.

4670.belief: Mixed media just means using any random materials together, it doesn’t really matter what you choose.
4670.statement: Mixed media just means using any random materials together, it doesn’t really matter what you choose.
4670.correction: Mixed media is intentional. Each material or technique is chosen for a reason, either to add texture, create contrast, or express an idea or emotion. Artists think carefully about how the materials work together to enhance the artwork.

5296.belief: You can paint over a mistake with a darker colour to fix it.
5296.statement: You can paint over a mistake with a darker colour to fix it.
5296.correction: In watercolour, layering too many dark colours can muddy the painting. It’s better to plan ahead, work from light to dark and use clean water and controlled layers to avoid errors.

3374.belief: Graphic communication is mainly about making things look pretty.
3374.statement: Graphic communication is mainly about making things look pretty.
3374.correction: While aesthetics are important, graphic communication focuses on conveying information effectively through visual principles like balance, hierarchy and alignment.

3068.belief: All fonts communicate the same message - it’s just about how the letters look.
3068.statement: All fonts communicate the same message - it’s just about how the letters look.
3068.correction: Fonts are like voices - each has a different tone. Choosing a bold, heavy font versus a thin, elegant one can completely change how a brand is perceived by the viewer.

4252.belief: Logos have to be complicated and detailed to look professional.
4252.statement: Logos have to be complicated and detailed to look professional.
4252.correction: The most successful logos are often simple as clear designs are more memorable and versatile across different media, formats and sizes.

10985.belief: Wet media must always be fully controlled and neat to look professional.
10985.statement: Wet media must always be fully controlled and neat to look professional.
10985.correction: Expressive, loose, or even accidental marks can be intentional and valued in graphic communication, depending on the project's aims.

2522.belief: Dry media can only be used for fine, detailed work.
2522.statement: Dry media can only be used for fine, detailed work.
2522.correction: Dry media is highly versatile and can be used for bold, expressive textures and atmospheric effects, not just for precision.

2380.belief: Digital manipulation is cheating or inauthentic art.
2380.statement: Digital manipulation is cheating or inauthentic art.
2380.correction: Digital art is a legitimate medium, just like painting or drawing. It requires creative decisions and skill - manipulation is a method of artistic expression, not a shortcut.

10205.belief: Any text will work as long as it’s readable.
10205.statement: Any text will work as long as it’s readable.
10205.correction: Typography must be chosen and placed purposefully to support the tone, audience and message - readability is just the starting point.

2127.belief: A more crowded layout makes the design look more informative or detailed.
2127.statement: A more crowded layout makes the design look more informative or detailed.
2127.correction: More elements can overwhelm the viewer. Effective use of empty space and a clear hierarchy can increase impact and readability.

2046.belief: Copying or replicating an image is an appropriate way to use a source.
2046.statement: Copying or replicating an image is an appropriate way to use a source.
2046.correction: Influence means taking inspiration and transforming it into something new, adding your own creative input rather than directly copying.

5812.belief: The principles of textiles only apply to fashion.
5812.statement: The principles of textiles only apply to fashion
5812.correction: The principles of textiles apply to interiors, art, and technical textiles.

344.correction: Stitching fabric shapes onto a background is a common way to attach pieces in appliqué. However, appliqué can also involve using fabric glue or PVA glue to attach smaller pieces of fabric to a larger background.

5568.belief: Plastic bags cannot be used in weaving because they are too soft.
5568.statement: Plastic bags cannot be used in weaving because they are too soft.
5568.correction: Nearly all materials can be used to weave with as long as they are cut correctly so that they can fit into the loom.

2456.belief: You don’t have to iron off the wax after dyeing.
2456.statement: You don’t have to iron off the wax after dyeing.
2456.correction: If you don't iron off the wax after dyeing, the fabric will look unfinished and waxy.

10643.belief: You can only use a sewing machine for straight lines or joining fabric.
10643.statement: You can only use a sewing machine for straight lines or joining fabric.
10643.correction: With a freehand arm, you can move the fabric in any direction to draw curves, lines, and patterns with thread. Artists use this to stitch portraits, text, and textures, guiding the fabric by hand like drawing with a pencil.

3442.belief: Hand stitching is only for old-fashioned or traditional designs.
3442.statement: Hand stitching is only for old-fashioned or traditional designs.
3442.correction: Hand stitching is a versatile skill that allows designers to add personal, creative and intricate details that machines often can’t replicate. It’s valued in modern fashion and art for its unique, handmade quality.

10065.belief: Surface pattern decoration is only used in textiles.
10065.statement: Surface pattern decoration is only used in textiles.
10065.correction: Surface pattern can be applied to many materials, including ceramics, wallpaper, furniture, and architecture.

9458.belief: A source is just something to copy.
9458.statement: A source is just something to copy.
9458.correction: Sources are not meant to be copied. They act as a starting point for creativity. Designers explore a source’s shapes, patterns, colours, or meanings and reinterpret them to create original work that reflects their own ideas and context.

5491.belief: Phones produce high quality photos, so photography with cameras is redundant.
5491.statement: Phones produce high quality photos, so photography with cameras is redundant
